cities.d: The reunified and reinvigorated capital of Germany; a metropolis of diversity with some of the world's best-known clubs, shops, galleries and restaurants.

x.around: Pedestrians should be careful not to walk in the designated bike lanes.

hidden.d: The "Small Müggelsee" is southeast of the "Large Müggelsee". Its sloping sand beach, which is called Strandbad Kleiner Müggelsee is one of the most popular bathing beaches in this southeast corner of Berlin, if not the most…
In the Köpenick Palace.
A multimedia museum documenting Berlin's history. You can also visit an underground bunker with room for over 3000 people.
Official website (in German). A museum of Berlin's different police forces through the ages, displaying historic uniforms, weapons, and specialist equipment such as cameras.
Varying exhibitions.

Not far away from Schloss Tegel (at the "große Malche") you can take a look at the oldest tree in Berlin, an oak which has been growing there since about 1192 (so it's actually older than Berlin itself).
The building of one of Berlin’s oldest breweries is a ravishingly beautiful and heritage-protected industrial monument.
The Schöneweide forced labor camp (GBI-Lager 75/76) on Britzer Straße is a complete ensemble, which makes it a rather unusual site in Berlin.

n.it: Centro di documentazione sul lavoro forzato nazista

x.intro: Berlin is Germany's capital and largest city. Within the city limits, Berlin in 2022 had a population of 3.7 million. Berlin is coming into its own again as a cosmopolitan capital of one of Europe's wealthiest nations. "Arm aber sexy" (poor but sexy), as a former mayor would have it, Berlin attracts young people, students, and a creative bohème like few other cities in the world.

must.d: Built by Hitler for the 1936 Olympic Games, this is one of the better examples of Nazi neoclassical architecture (laying claim to the legacy of Rome, fasces and all) and is still used for sporting events.

This museum explains how this house was used for a meeting of senior Nazis to ensure that they all knew that the SS would industrialize the use of mass-murder in disposing of Jews and "undesirables" and to debate a little the…
One of the oldest buildings in Charlottenburg and actually the reason for the whole city to be built.
Also known as "der hohle Zahn" (the Hollow Tooth), this church in Breitscheidplatz is a memorial to Kaiser Wilhelm, and one of Berlin's most famous landmarks.

The "mother of all airports", according to Sir Norman Foster, is a huge relic of the interwar era. The terminal building, built between 1936 and 1941 immediately south of the city centre, was the hot spot of the Berlin airlift…
The old town of Köpenick is surrounded by water. Especially noteworthy are the Köpenick Palace which houses a museum of applied art and the Neogothic town hall.

The zoo in the former East Berlin is more spacious than its West Berlin counterpart, the historic Berlin Zoo and has been open for some 50 years. The Tierpark has nearly as many animals, but fewer reptiles and aquatic animals.
The garden is part of the Free University of Berlin.

n.ar: متحف حديقة النباتات والأشجار في داهلم
n.de: Botanischer Garten und Botanisches Museum Berlin
n.en: Botanical Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem

next.d: (35 km) — the capital of the surrounding federal state of Brandenburg, not far southwest of Berlin, and makes a perfect day trip.
(35 km) — a quiet suburb housing the remains of KZ Sachsenhausen, one of the few preserved Nazi concentration camps on German soil. There's also a small palace in the centre of Oranienburg.
(c. 85 km) — a protected UNESCO biosphere reserve. It includes low-lying areas in which the river Spree meanders in thousands of small waterways through meadows and forests.
(100 km) — on the Polish border, with many international students, is within easy reach. Just over an hour by RE train (half-hourly service).
(110 km) — about 40 minutes southwest of Berlin by ICE. Schlosskirche was the church where Martin Luther nailed his theses to the church door, starting the Protestant Reformation.
and Central German Lake District about as far to the south as the Baltic is to the north - former lignite pits turned into artificial lakes
(190 km) — East Germany's most vibrant and fastest-growing city, known for its creative cultural scene, sometimes pretentiously called the "New Berlin", but still a lot smaller and more relaxed than…
(190 km) — the former royal capital of Saxony with its Baroque palaces, churches and precious art treasures; two hours by train or car to the south.

x.safe: Berlin might be a safe place, but it is a huge city, and as such has some not-so-well maintained areas. No specific rules apply with the exception of public transportation and tourist areas where pickpockets are a problem. Watch your bags during rush hours, at larger train stations (with the central and Warschauer stations being notoriously sketchy at night).

cities.d: Its old market, the Schnoor, the Böttcherstrasse, the Viertel and its maritime flair all make Bremen a great urban experience.

x.around: In the west lie the cities Delmenhorst and Oldenburg and the Frisian islands. In the east you can travel to Verden, in the south to Osnabrück.

hidden.d: Built on the site of the former city fortifications, this star-shaped park is the oldest public garden in Germany. It features scenic walking paths, colorful flowerbeds, and the historic "Am Wall" windmill.
The sports museum shows the history of the football club SV Werder Bremen. You can see photos, jerseys, trophies and more.
Housed in a former cotton warehouse. Models of ships used during the past.
Vintage steam & diesel trains operate over a 7.8 metric-gauge line.
Founded as a design museum but also used for exhibitions in modern art. The museum is named after Wilhelm Wagenfeld, an industrial designer born 1900 in Bremen.
A good overview of the history of Bremen City with a wide range of collections.
The contemporary art museum shows the work of Gerhard Marcks the sculptor of the statue "Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten", a city landmark.

x.intro: The Free Hanseatic City of Bremen is a city in northern Germany with a major port on the River Weser. The population is 567,000 (2020). It is also the name of one of the states of Germany which consists of two separated enclaves on the River Weser; the other enclave, Bremerhaven, is covered by its own article.

must.d: This is one of the finest in Europe and has been included on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Building work started in 1410 and it is seen as an important display of the wealth and freedom of the city.
This statue on the main square, in front of the town hall, is of the Knight Roland, subject of the Medieval epic, the Song of Roland, who was a protector of trade.
Over 1,200 years old, its huge towered façade dominates the main square. The interior is also impressive, with some fine painted details on the ceilings.

n.es: Catedral de San Pedro de Bremen

must.d: Bremen's oldest district, characterized by narrow lanes and timber-framed houses dating back to the 15th and 16th centuries.
An incredible Jugendstil (Art Nouveau) street that runs from the main square towards the river. There are many fine façades and courtyards all with large amounts of design detail.
Science museum with plenty of interactive exhibits such as an earthquake simulator. The main building is a huge steel shell designed by the Bremen architect Thomas Klumpp.

x.safe: The area close to the railway station is rough late at night, and it may also be a bit spooky to cross the Wallanlagen park then. Therefore, if you have to go from the old city to areas to its west or northwest late at night, consider taking a tram or bus instead of walking.

cities.d: (Köln) – Founded by the Romans 2000 years ago and known for its huge cathedral (second largest in the world), Romanesque churches, archaeological sites and the lively old town quarter.

x.around: Tickets are valid for subway, tram, bus and regional train within the VRS-network. Trips within the city limits require zone 1b tickets (2026: single €3.80, 4-trip-ticket €13.60, 24-hour ticket €9.20, 24-hour ticket for up to 5 people €18.60), week ticket €37.60. For short trips of up to 4 stops on subway, tram or bus there is also the slightly cheaper "Kurzstrecke" (short trip ticket, 2026: €2.30).

n.en: ruins of Roman city walls and two towers

hidden.d: This student neighbourhood takes its name from the Parisian Quartier Latin. It is centred on the Zülpicher Straße and provides ample nightlife opportunities, ranging from a night shop (Späti) with dancefloor and toilets, to grimy…
Old town between Rhine, Heumarkt, Alter Markt and Dom, (Cologne Cathedral).
The Praetorium served as the administrative headquarters of the Roman governor in Cologne, then the capital of the province of Germania Inferior.

x.intro: Cologne (German: Köln, Ripuarian: Kölle) is a city on the Rhine river in North Rhine-Westphalia. It is the fourth largest city in Germany with around 1.1 million residents (2025). It is one of the nation's media, tourism and business hotspots, and is considered one of the most liberal cities in Germany.

must.d: A UNESCO World Heritage site, this monumental cathedral took 632 years to complete, finally being consecrated in 1880. Cologne's Dom is the first thing you will notice when leaving through the main exit of the central station.
Also called the Locking Bridge. If you walk to the back of the Kölner Dom along a straight path, there is a bridge on the Rhine to your right that is covered in padlocks.
The Wallraf-Richartz Museum is an art gallery with a collection of fine art from the medieval period through to the early 20th century.
A museum of modern art, near the central railway station and the Cathedral hosts a worthy regular exhibition and temporary exhibitions.
Römisch-Germanisches Museum explores the history of Roman history in Cologne and the surrounding area. The permanent exhibition is now located in the Belgian House (Cäcilienstraße 46, near Neumarkt).

The Cologne Synagogue is architecturally striking for its dark, monumental style. Its Torah scroll has a significant history, having been rescued by a Catholic priest from another synagogue during the Nazi era.
One of Germany's oldest churches, built on the foundations of a late antique oval structure. It is famous for its unique decagonal dome and elliptical floor plan.

One of Germany's oldest continuously used churches, with origins dating back to the Roman era. It is best known for the "Golden Chamber," a historic ossuary, and its significance as a site of pilgrimage.

next.d: the former capital of West Germany is due south and easy to reach by train or Stadtbahn (Regional Express 5; MittelRheinBahn MRB 48; U-Bahn line 16 and 18; also ICEs, ICs, and EC's ).
almost a suburb of Cologne, contains the Augustusburg Palace which has been placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
The lively state capital that has quite some local rivalry with Cologne. Here you can find an old town carefully rebuilt after WWII and nice outdoor bars along the Rhine.
A small town reachable by train; the main sight here is the Drachenburg Castle.
(Ruhrgebiet) — If you are interested in heavy industry this might be a worthwhile trip. It is about 100 km north of Cologne.
a small town southwest of Cologne dating from Roman times. It has a newly opened museum centred on Roman baths and bathing culture. It is also a gateway to the forested hills of the Eifel region.

x.safe: Cologne's safety levels are historically average by German standards, but since the mid-2010s, the city has been plagued with significant waves of crime and decay.

cities.d: Once called "Florence on the Elbe", known for the Frauenkirche (the finest baroque cathedral outside Italy) and its historic Altstadt, that were both rebuilt after being destroyed during World War…

x.around: Dresden has an extensive reliable and high quality (even by German standards) public transport system consisting of regional railways (called S-Bahn, historically Schnellbahn), trams (called Straßenbahn) and buses. Three ferries cross the Elbe and two cable car systems go up Loschwitz hill. The Straßenbahn and S-Bahn are two entirely separate networks, although there are tram stops at many S-Bahn stations.

hidden.d: The music conservatoire hosts regular concerts and events at various venues.

n.en: Hochschule für Musik Carl Maria von Weber Dresden

hidden.d: Real baroque houses. The quarter reaches from the "Heinrichstraße" up to the "Albert Platz". On the Heinrichstr and in the surroundings you will find a lot of antique stores.
The remains of the old fort. Gives you a glimpse of what a fort in a medieval European town was like.
The building was used as a studio and museum by the artist Eduard Leonhardi (late Romanticism) until he died in 1905.
Two buildings in the middle of Neustadt with many small stores and some bars, many of them in the artistically decorated inner courtyards.
Art from Dresden and the region with a main focus on the 20th century to the present. The collection also contains pieces of art dating back until the 16th century.
Go to the (mostly) green river banks, especially on hot summer evenings/nights for a very nice view of the old parts and lot of people playing sports, having barbecues and parties.
Impressive building for the arts constructed in the 19th century. The Kunsthalle is part of the Dresden State Art Collections (SKD).

x.intro: Dresden is the capital of Saxony (Sachsen). It's often referred to locally as Elbflorenz, or "Florence on the Elbe", reflecting its location on the Elbe river and its historical role as a centre for the arts and beautiful architecture – much like Florence in Italy.

must.d: The original Church of Our Lady was completely destroyed during World War II; however, it has been reconstructed. The City of Coventry, which was raided by the Luftwaffe in WWII, donated the golden cross for the dome of the…

The baroque palace features a nympheum, many sculptures of Permoser, a bell pavilion and famous art collections. Do not miss the "Alte Meister" - you'll find Rafael's famous Sistine Madonna with its well-known angels there.
This opera house is known for its architecture and the Staatskapelle Dresden orchestra. Its history includes the premieres of several operas by Wagner and Strauss.

A highly regarded collection featuring around 700 European works from the 15th to the 18th century. It is particularly known for its focus on Italian Renaissance and Baroque art, including Raphael's Sistine Madonna, as well as a…

During the bombing of Dresden in February 1945 the interior of the palace was almost completely destroyed by fire. Only the part that is now the Historisches Grünes Gewölbe (and the basements) was unaffected.

n.fr: château de la Résidence de Dresde

must.d: One of the most significant collections of European goldsmith's work and decorative arts. The museum is divided into two sections, each requiring a separate ticket.
This biggest porcelain painting of the world shows (almost) all Saxon princes, electors and kings on their horses and splendid parade uniforms.
The "Balcony of Europe" stretches for 500 m along the River Elbe, some 10 m over the water table, and being up to 20 m wide.

next.d: (8 km northwest) is a city west of Dresden which includes the Karl May Museum (dedicated to the famous writer) and its vineyards

(14 km northwest) has a beautiful castle that was once used when the kings went hunting. Reachable by a charming historic narrow gauge railway from Radebeul or (more mundanely but faster) by bus from…
(25 km northwest) has a medieval cathedral and castle and home to the first European porcelain factory. Residence of the Saxon dukes and electors before they moved to Dresden.
(Erzgebirge) has hiking and crafts (toymaking, especially Christmas toys)
(Sächsische Schweiz) is upstream along the river Elbe is a national park for hiking and rock-climbing
(40 km southeast) has one of the largest and best preserved late medieval fortresses in Europe. The Königstein fortress is situated about 30 km from Dresden and can be reached by almost all means of…

x.safe: Dresden is a safe place to be, just like the rest of Germany. Avoid visiting the Alaunpark in the night. Be careful in the Neustadt after midnight; don't use small dark streets.

cities.d: Germany's capital of shopping that also has a wide variety of fascinating new architecture. The "Altstadt" quarter and the Rhine embankments have a vibrant nightlife.

x.around: As of 2026, fares for Category A are for a single ticket and for a 24-hour pass. Children under 15 pay a flat rate of per journey. Tickets can be purchased via the Rheinbahn, VRR, or DB apps; at customer service centers; from ticket machines at stops; and from bus drivers (contactless payment preferred).

hidden.d: At the old town limits next to Rhine. Here was the erstwhile castle of the Earls of Berg, the later duke of Jülich-Kleve-Berg. The castle was later reconstructed as a baroque palace, which burned down in 1872.
Heine (1797-1856) was a poet and author and perhaps the most famed Düsseldorfer in German history
The Carlsplatz is the centre of Carlstadt and houses the city's only permanent weekday market, featuring savory food, sweets, flowers as well as popular artworks

On the right hand of the monument is a little river, named the northern Düssel. It gave the city its name (Düsseldorf means village at Düssel). The balustrade is an artwork of Bert Gerreshein too. It is also full of symbols.

The historic and striking city hall of Düsseldorf dates from the 16th century. Since then it has housed the city parliament. The building consists of three parts, and there are guided tours for free every Wednesday at 15:00.
This clock also shows the current water level in the river.
An artwork of Bert Gerresheim, donated by the society “Düsseldorfer Jonges” on occasion of the 700th anniversary of the foundation of the town.

x.intro: Düsseldorf is a city on the River Rhine in western Germany and is the capital city of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is one of the economic centres of the country, and a major city within the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan area, with a population of 660,000 (2025).

must.d: The population of the Rhinelands is mainly Catholic, and Protestants and members of the Reformed Church had to suffer many restrictions. Finally, the Contract of Rheinberg 1682 granted everybody the free practice of religion.

next.d: the largest city in North Rhine-Westphalia maintaining a legendary rivalry with its close neighbour
almost a suburb of Cologne and contains the Augustusburg Palace which has been placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
the former capital of (West) Germany is due south and easy to reach by train or S-Bahn
and Bad Honnef — small towns at the Middle Rhine Valley reachable by train
with the towns of Neuss, Meerbusch and Krefeld
(Ruhrgebiet) — If you are interested in heavy industry and/or industrial culture this might be a worthwhile trip. It is about 50 km north of Düsseldorf.
city known for the hanging monorail from 1901, Schwebebahn.

x.safe: Düsseldorf is generally as safe as other European cities of similar size. However the surroundings of the central railway station might be a bit intimidating, particularly at night, if there are junkies around. In particular, the pedestrianised office district outside the rear entrance to the station, heading away from the town centre, is quite deserted late at night and best avoided.

cities.d: A magnificent skyline, financial and transportation hub of Europe, headquarters of the European Central Bank (ECB) and an important trade fair.

x.around: Frankfurt has a good, co-ordinated public transport system of Underground (U-Bahn), tram (Straßenbahn) and bus. Public transit nerds will be quick to point out, that the "U-Bahn" is actually a bit of a misnomer, given the fact that it has moved traffic sections in the outskirts, more in line with systems called "Stadtbahn" in other German cities.
x.intro: Frankfurt (German, and sometimes in English: Frankfurt am Main) is the largest city in the German state of Hesse, and is considered the business and financial centre of Germany. It is the fifth largest city in Germany after Berlin, Hamburg, Munich and Cologne. The city is known for its modern skyline, and for hosting the headquarters of the European Central Bank, the Deutsche Börse stock exchange and numerous German financial services companies.

must.d: As one of Europe's busiest hubs, the airport offers behind-the-scenes insights. Guided tours provide access to the airfield and specialized areas, such as the impressive fire department facilities.
A remarkably preserved medieval area with half-timbered houses and narrow streets. Key highlights include the 9th-century St.
Established in 1858, this is one of the oldest zoos in the world. It gained international fame under the direction of Bernhard Grzimek, who pioneered animal conservation.
Unlike the city center, Bornheim largely survived the war intact, preserving its charming medieval and baroque half-timbered houses.
An old 43-metre wooden tower with viewing platform offering nice views of the skyline. It burned down in 2017, but has since been rebuilt.

next.d: Gutenberg's home on the Rhine, with a well-preserved old city, 45 min by S-Bahn
wealthy historic spa city and state capital, 45 minutes by S-Bahn , , or 35 min. by SE10 from Hauptbahnhof
at the southern end of the Rhine Valley and the Rheingau, 73 min by SE10.
former residence of the duchy of Hesse, picturesque old town, art nouveau architecture
spa town with close by old Roman fort Saalburg that is on the UNESCO heritage list
Small city with a picturesque medieval Altstadt (old town area).
art nouveau buildings and place where Elvis Presley stayed while in the Army (1958-1960)
with famous castle and charming old town, 55 min by IC.

x.safe: Frankfurt has one of Germany's highest crime rates, though, in part, only for statistical reasons: smuggling and similar offences at the airport as well as anything concerning credit card fraud anywhere in Germany is registered in Frankfurt, since the main credit card clearing company is based in the city.

cities.d: Germany's second-largest city is known for its harbour, its numerous channels and bridges, the Speicherstadt, the Michel church and the new Elbphilharmonie concert hall, the bustling nightlife around…

x.around: Hamburg's city centre is not particularly large, and getting around on foot is perfectly doable when visiting attractions in the centre. However, Hamburg as a whole is quite extensive (over 700 km²), and some attractions are in the outlying districts. Fortunately, it has an excellent public transport system, which makes it easy to reach nearly every part of the city, as well as many surrounding areas.

hidden.d: Hamburg's impressive city hall was built in 1897 out of sandstone in neo-Renaissance style, including a 112-m tower. The square in front of the city hall is the Rathausmarkt, hosting many events especially in summer.
Ensemble of traditional half-timbered merchant houses.
The house, depicting the form of a ship, is probably the best example of the 1920s style of "Kontorhaus" architecture. Large office buildings are displayed in the typical, northern red brick style.
Hamburg's oldest remaining bridge from the 17th century
Look at the erecting process from an orange observation tower, which allows nice views on the HafenCity, the harbour, and the river.
The building of the Patriotic Society was erected following the great fire of 1842 on the former site of the old town hall of Hamburg.
Here you can find information about the new buildings and the whole district. The InfoCenter also provides free guided tours.
Dating from the beginning of the 20th century as most buildings around, but looking much older.

x.intro: This article refers to the city of Hamburg. For the island of Neuwerk that is part of the state of Hamburg but not the city see there

must.d: New 'architectural lighthouse' of Hamburg. On the top of a huge old warehouse a 110 metres tall modern philharmonic hall with glass façade and wave-shaped roof.

Hamburg's massive container ports line the southern bank of the river Elbe. They are most spectacular at night, and the best place to view them from is by driving north along the A7 highway (heading into the Elbtunnel tunnel).

All five main churches of Hamburg were damaged in World War II. But in contrast to the other four, St. Nikolai has not been re-erected making it a memorial against war. It was designed by English architect George Gilbert Scott.
A street and entertainment district in Hamburg's St. Pauli district, one of the two centres of Hamburg's nightlife (with Schanze) and also the city's major red-light district.

The world's largest model railway layout. The panoramas include parts of Hamburg, the Alps, the American west, South America, and a Scandinavian exhibit which features automated ships on a body of water.
The youngest and most famous of the five is also the only baroque church. This building is not the original St. Michaelis - that one (built 1647-1669) was destroyed by a lightning strike in 1750.

Hamburg's Zoo. The collection began in 1863 with animals that belonged to Carl Hagenbeck Sr. (1810–1887), a fishmonger who became an amateur animal collector. The park itself was founded by Carl Hagenbeck Jr. in 1907.
The astrophysics faculty of the Universität Hamburg is spread over a big park with protected neobaroque buildings with historical equipment for astronomy science including different telescopes.

next.d: A hanseatic city 95 km away, famous for the Bremer Stadtmusikanten (Town Musicians of Bremen).
Germany's most off-shore North Sea island. Reachable by express ferry from St. Pauli Landungsbrücken.
Kiel's main tourist attraction is the "Kieler Woche" (Kiel Week) at the end of June, the largest sailing event in the world and one of Germany's largest festivals.
The city is connected to the Baltic Sea by the Trave river. The old city (Altstadt) survived from medieval times and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage List.
A city in Lower Saxony, about 50 km southeast of Hamburg. Like Lübeck, Lüneburg's old town has kept a medieval look with old buildings and narrow streets.
The old town at the Baltic Sea maintained its sleepy character despite the fact that at weekends there are loads of tourists.

x.safe: Hamburg is a very safe city, and as long as you are aware of your surroundings and use common sense, there are no areas which are dangerous to be in, even at night.

cities.d: (München) – Germany's third-largest city and booming capital of Bavaria is known for the Oktoberfest, the Hofbräuhaus, its manifold cultural offerings including operas, theatres and museums, a…

x.around: The innermost city is walkable and the outer fringes are suitable for a car. For everything else use the excellent public transport system.

hidden.d: Omitting Europe and Antarctica, the former Museum für Völkerkunde is a global ethnological collection.
This Roman Catholic church is opposite the main building of the University of Munich (LMU Munich). It's in Romanesque style, and features the second-largest altar fresco in the world.
History of the festival, in a townhouse of 1340. The "Himmelsleiter" is its characteristic early staircase, a straight flight with no corners.
This branch of Deutsches Museum is about transport of every kind. The main themes are urban transport, travel, and mobility and technology.
Small display of life in the neighbourhood. Exhibitions have varying hours and prices.
Changing art exhibitions provided by the art foundation of Versicherungskammer Bayern.
Striking modern Roman Catholic church completed in 1953. Even more striking are the five bells, which are trying their best to be heard in Hamburg.
Modern art museum, no permanent collection but rotating exhibitions. It's funded by HypoVereinsbank.

n.it: Galleria d'arte della Fondazione Hypo per la cultura

x.intro: Munich (German: München, Bavarian: Minga) is the capital of the federal state of Bavaria in the south of Germany. Within the city limits, Munich in 2024 has a population of just under 1.6 million, the third most populous city in Germany. Greater Munich including its suburbs has a population of 3 million. The Munich metropolitan region, which encompasses cities such as Augsburg and Ingolstadt, has a population of 6.2 million.

must.d: Enormous museum of science and technology, needing a full day, and even then you need to prioritise which galleries to explore - though half the fun is discovering the secrets of technology you'd never considered.
What began as a modest 17th century pavilion grew and grew into a vast Baroque palace, bigger than Versailles, which was no accident.
Contains hundreds of great European masterworks dating from the 14th to the 18th centuries, including the largest Rubens collection in the world. Café Klenze is its pleasant bakery cafe.

This huge church defines the Munich skyline with its twin onion-domed towers, a shade over 98 m tall - the money ran out for the planned spires. It's the Roman Catholic cathedral, but always known locally as Frauenkirche.

n.es: Catedral de Nuestra Señora de Múnich

must.d: This houses King Ludwig I's huge collection of Greek and Roman sculpture: he was determined to make Munich into a new Athens, if necessary by removing the original Athens piece by piece.
Royal Palace and seat of government of the Wittelsbach dynasty, bombed in wartime but rebuilt. The two principal areas are the Treasury and the Museum (separate admission €9 each).
Humonguous complex of three palaces. The Old Palace at the west end was a mansion built up into a palace only to be promptly scrapped and rebuilt by 1623.

Early 19th century Bavaria was a pawn in conflicts between Austria and Napoleonic France, so when Ludwig I came to the throne in 1825, he sought an iconic statue to symbolise Bavaria's strength and independence, and a hall of…

n.en: Bavaria statue and Hall of Fame

next.d: has a monastery in a beautiful setting above the Ammersee, with a famous brewery and beer garden.
has a large lake with a castle and a monastery on its islands.
is best known for its concentration camp, now a museum, but also has a Renaissance palace.
at the foot of the Alps is dominated by Neuschwanstein, the "Disney-castle" in all the tourist brochures, and equally-interesting Hohenschwangau.
is an Alpine resort. Take the rack railway to the top of Zugspitze, Germany's highest mountain.
is a medieval walled city with many outstanding museums, including coverage of the Nazi era and its downfall.
is a beautiful medieval city and on the Danube.
in Austria is a historic city with Hohensalzburg Fortress glowering above.

x.safe: Boasting one of the lowest crime rates of any major European city, Munich is a very safe city, and violent crime is rare. Walking around, day or night, is not an issue, and you will most likely not encounter any crime at all, though you should still take the usual precautions against pickpocketing (especially in the central districts of Altstadt-Lehel and the Ludwigsvorstadt area immediately south of the central…

cities.d: (Nürnberg) – A former Reichsstadt with a medieval touch, its old town was partly reconstructed after severe bombing in the war, including the Gothic Kaiserburg and the major churches.

x.around: The old town is best explored on foot. To get from one part of the old town to another by car or public transport, you will often have to leave the old town and reenter it at a different gate.

hidden.d: 14th-century graveyard with many famous citizens, including Albrecht Dürer and Adam Kraft. In summer the gardens are a riot of roses and other colourful flowers.

In the Middle Ages, cities like Nuremberg were strongly protected by walls and castles, but villages lacked them. It was often impractical to build these around a straggling farm village, and the cities jealously guarded their…

Built in Romanesque style from the 13th century, with many later Gothic and Baroque additions, and now part of the Evangelical or Lutheran church of Germany, St Sebaldhus is the focus of the north-side old town.
The western and most prestigious part, grouped around the inner courtyard. It was the temporary residence of the Holy Roman Emperors.
A museum dedicated to preserving the history of board games with many original games, some of which can be played by visitors.
Trams since they began here in 1881. Several are in working order and when the museum is open, they make a leisurely grinding circuit of the city's public tramways.
Interactive science museum with emphasis on human perceptionClosed during Winter (17 Dec to 1 Mar)
Hosts changing art exhibitions. Entry is free on Wednesdays, 18:00–20:00.

x.intro: Nuremberg (German: Nürnberg) is Franconia's largest city, and its undisputed economic, social and cultural centre. The city lies on the Pegnitz River and the Main-Danube Canal. Within the city limits Nuremberg has a population of about 520,000 (2018), making it the second-biggest city in the Bundesland Bavaria and the biggest city in the region of Franconia. Greater Nuremberg including its suburbs has a population of 1.3 million.

must.d: The Nuremberg Castle is the rambling fortification that dominates the old town. While it appears to be one massive fortress, it historically consists of three distinct parts that often stood in conflict with one another.
One of the largest museum of art and crafts in the German-speaking countries, with a collection ranging from pre-historic artefacts to 20th century art. Allow at least half a day.
Mostly built in the 15th century and now part of the Evangelical or Lutheran church of Germany, Lorenzkirche forms the focus of the south-side old town.
The house in which the painter Albrecht Dürer lived and worked from 1509 until 1528. Representative of a wealthy house of that period. Exhibition about life in the house and the way Dürer worked.
The Nuremberg Tiergarten is one of the most beautiful zoos in Europe, set in forests and old quarries to the east of the city. Includes a Dolphinarium with regular shows.

After World War II, this site was chosen for trials of the Nazi high command, partly for Nuremberg's symbolic role in Nazism, but chiefly because the Palace of Justice was undamaged and contained a prison block.
Within Old Town but in a striking modern building, the museum shows art and design from 1945 to today.

n.en: Neues Museum ("New Museum", State Museum for Art and Design in Nürnberg)

next.d: just 5 km west, this has charming medieval streets, a Jewish museum and a radio museum.
University town with a remarkable collection of museums and early modern architecture (and, of course, bicycles cranked by earnest young men and women).
pleasant old town centre.
once an ecclesiastical centre, the entire town is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its original Romanesque buildings, which survived the war. Its beer is also famous.
even if you don't care for opera, admire its baroque centre and collection of palaces. Tickets for the annual Wagner Opera Festival get snapped up months in advance.
is packed with medieval, Renaissance and baroque architecture.
astride the Danube and still showing traces of its Roman founders, the city sights reflect its status as a former capital of Bavaria.

x.safe: According to the state police, Nuremberg has the lowest crime rate of the cities with more than 400,000 inhabitants.

intro: Germany (German: Deutschland) is the largest country in Central Europe. It is known for its rich cultural heritage, innovative inventions, its old-world charm and Gemütlichkeit (cosiness). Discard any perceptions of Germany as being homogeneous; a country of surprising regional diversity awaits your presence. Many tourists visit Germany to experience European history and the diverse German landscape.

other.d: (Ostseeküste) – Once the playground for crowned heads, this region is coming into its own again after the Cold War shut much of it off from the wider world.

x.around: In order to explore the Baltic Sea Coast you can use public means of transport such as trains. Also bikes can be used to make trips in defined regions. During the high season the roads on the islands of Rügen and Usedom tend to be overcrowded. Traffic jams are a common experience on Saturdays.
x.intro: The Baltic Sea Coast (Ostseeküste) of Germany is a vacation region located in the northern federal states of Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The eastern part of it is known as the German Riviera. Besides the obvious draw of a beach destination, many of the old towns in this area bear witness to the former wealth of Hanseatic cities and are well worth a visit.
x.safe: The crime rate is comparably low at the Baltic Sea Coast. Only bicycle theft and right-wing extremist criminal acts are quite common in particular in the eastern area of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

other.d: (Bayerische Alpen) – Germany perhaps at its most clichéd, but also its most beautiful; nice skiing in winter, hiking in summer and Schloss Neuschwanstein are just the most obvious attractions.

x.around: Considering the rural and mountainous nature of the region, the area's rail network is well established and its hub is in Munich. There are many connections to neighbouring Innsbruck and Salzburg in Austria. The road system is excellent as well and offers wonderful opportunities for road biking.
x.intro: The Bavarian Alps are part of the Alps and are located in Germany at the southern end of the federal state of Bavaria and continue across the border into Austria. The region is considered one of the most beautiful landscapes of Germany and ranks as one of the most scenic places in all of Central Europe. This is where German or Bavarian stereotypes of lederhosen, dirndls, weißwurst, and glistening alpine peaks come true.
x.safe: There are no major cities in the Bavarian Alps so dangerous drivers and mountain roads and wildlife may be your only real concern. Mountain safety is the key when going to higher altitudes as every year tourists die in accidents because of reckless behaviour and poor planning.

other.d: (Schwarzwald) – You are likely to think "cuckoo clock" or cherry pie, and you'd be forgiven, but there is much more to this region than that.

x.around: The region is covered by regional trains and buses. As they can be infrequent, it is better to check the departure times in advance (e.g., through bahn.de or some public transport apps).
x.intro: The Black Forest (German: Schwarzwald) is in the south-west corner of Germany in the federal state of Baden-Württemberg, which contains the namesake low, forested mountain range and warm, sunny lowlands at its foot. It is known as one of Germany's most beautiful and favourite destinations.

next.d: follow the tracks of the world's first return car journey back in 1888 from Pforzheim in the Black Forest to Mannheim
and enjoy some Spätzle egg noodles in this picturesque adjoining region that joins Baden-Württemberg with Bavaria.

other.d: (Ostfriesische Inseln) – Among Germany's most popular summer holiday spots, those largely car free islands in the Wadden Sea still see less international visitors than they deserve.

x.intro: The East Frisian Islands (German: Ostfriesische Inseln) are part of Lower Saxony, and part of the Wadden Sea UNESCO World Heritage Site. The seven inhabited islands attract summer visitors and sun worshippers. Those seeking peace and solitude, however, are best off during the colder months.

next.d: is probably the most popular excursion, other than that there are few options for onward travel that don't boil down to going back to the mainland.

other.d: (Fränkische Schweiz) – A favourite with early 19th-century poets who gave a name that stuck, this karst region is world renowned for its climbing and has some beautiful caves.

x.around: The area is surprisingly underserved by public transport and its roads are prone to congestion on weekends in the summer. There are however, good hiking and bike trails if you are fit enough to manage the steep slopes.

hidden.d: Run by the same people that also run Burg Rabenstein, a nearby castle, this cave offers breathtaking limestone formations and an honest to god, real cave bear skeleton that was discovered on site.
The scenic railway from Ebermannstadt to Behringersmühle was converted into a heritage railway when commercial services stopped.

x.intro: The Franconian Switzerland (German: Fränkische Schweiz) is an upland in Franconia, northern Bavaria and a popular tourist retreat. It is one of the oldest and most popular holiday areas in Germany.
x.safe: The biggest hazards in this region are natural. When climbing or canoeing you should apply general rules of safety to minimize any risk of injury or accident. Other than that, this region is as safe as it can get.
